claim: Secretins form large macromolecular complexes which assemble in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Proteins of the secretin family form large macromolecular complexes, which assemble in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about secretin proteins.

claim: Secretins are major components of type II and III secretion systems.
source: Secretins are major components of type II and III secretion systems and are linked to extrusion of type IV pili (T4P) and to DNA uptake.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Secretins are linked to extrusion of type IV pili (T4P).
source: Secretins are major components of type II and III secretion systems and are linked to extrusion of type IV pili (T4P) and to DNA uptake.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Secretins are linked to DNA uptake.
source: Secretins are major components of type II and III secretion systems and are linked to extrusion of type IV pili (T4P) and to DNA uptake.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The in situ structure of a T4P molecular machine was determined in the open and closed state by electron cryo-tomography of whole Thermus thermophilus cells.
source: By electron cryo-tomography of whole Thermus thermophilus cells, we determined the in situ structure of a T4P molecular machine in the open and the closed state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal domains of the central secretin PilQ shift by approximately 30 Å during the conformational change between closed and open states.
source: Comparison reveals a major conformational change whereby the N-terminal domains of the central secretin PilQ shift by ∼30 Å, and two periplasmic gates open to make way for pilus extrusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Two periplasmic gates open to make way for pilus extrusion during the conformational change.
source: Comparison reveals a major conformational change whereby the N-terminal domains of the central secretin PilQ shift by ∼30 Å, and two periplasmic gates open to make way for pilus extrusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The structure of the assembled pilus was determined.
source: Furthermore, we determine the structure of the assembled pilus.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Secretins form multimeric pores through the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Secretins form multimeric pores through the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria (Averhoff, 2009; Korotkov et al., 2011; Burkhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Secretins are the central secretion conduits for proteins and virulence factors in type II and III secretion systems.
source: They are the central secretion conduits for proteins and virulence factors in type II and III secretion systems (T2SS/T3SS) and are essential for extrusion of type IV pili (T4P) (Martin et al., 1993) and transport of some bacteriophages (Korotkov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Secretins are essential for extrusion of type IV pili (T4P).
source: They are the central secretion conduits for proteins and virulence factors in type II and III secretion systems (T2SS/T3SS) and are essential for extrusion of type IV pili (T4P) (Martin et al., 1993) and transport of some bacteriophages (Korotkov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 1993.

claim: Secretins are involved in transport of some bacteriophages.
source: They are the central secretion conduits for proteins and virulence factors in type II and III secretion systems (T2SS/T3SS) and are essential for extrusion of type IV pili (T4P) (Martin et al., 1993) and transport of some bacteriophages (Korotkov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Korotkov et al., 2011.

claim: Secretins are key components of DNA transport systems which mediate uptake of free DNA from the environment, referred to as natural transformation.
source: In addition, secretins are key components of DNA transport systems, which mediate uptake of free DNA from the environment, referred to as natural transformation (Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: The ability to take up DNA is one of the major mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer.
source: The ability to take up DNA is one of the major mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer (Domingues et al., 2012) and enables organisms to adapt rapidly to changing environments (Averhoff, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Domingues et al., 2012.

claim: DNA uptake enables organisms to adapt rapidly to changing environments.
source: The ability to take up DNA is one of the major mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer (Domingues et al., 2012) and enables organisms to adapt rapidly to changing environments (Averhoff, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Averhoff, 2009.

claim: Natural transformation is fundamental for adaptation of pathogenic bacteria to human hosts and the acquisition of multi-drug resistance.
source: This process is also fundamental for adaptation of pathogenic bacteria to human hosts and the acquisition of multi-drug resistance (Domingues et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Domingues et al., 2012.

claim: In many Gram-negative bacteria such as Thermus, Neisseria, Pseudomonas, and Vibrio, DNA uptake is linked to the T4P machinery.
source: In many Gram-negative bacteria, such as Thermus, and also in many major human pathogens such as Neisseria, Pseudomonas, and Vibrio, DNA uptake is linked to the T4P machinery (Wolfgang et al., 1998; Graupner et al., 2000; Seitz and Blokesch, 2013) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wolfgang et al., 1998; Graupner et al., 2000; Seitz and Blokesch, 2013.

claim: Thermus thermophilus HB27 exhibits the highest transformation rates known to date.
source: To investigate the structure and function of this system, we chose the thermophilic bacterium Thermus thermophilus HB27, which exhibits the highest transformation rates known to date (Koyama et al., 1986), and due to the thermostability of its proteins is a convenient model for structural studies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koyama et al., 1986.

claim: Thermus thermophilus HB27 is a convenient model for structural studies due to the thermostability of its proteins.
source: To investigate the structure and function of this system, we chose the thermophilic bacterium Thermus thermophilus HB27, which exhibits the highest transformation rates known to date (Koyama et al., 1986), and due to the thermostability of its proteins is a convenient model for structural studies.
evidence: This is based on the known thermostability of proteins from thermophilic organisms.

claim: The type IV pilus machinery is a heterooligomer formed from at least 10 different proteins.
source: The type IV pilus machinery is a heterooligomer, formed from at least 10 different proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: The PilQ secretin forms a channel in the outer membrane for secretion of the pilus-forming protein PilA4.
source: The PilQ secretin (orange) forms a channel in the outer membrane for secretion of the pilus-forming protein PilA4 (green), which is processed by the prepillin peptidase PilD (grey) (Friedrich et al., 2002; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by citations to Friedrich et al., 2002; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: PilA4 is processed by the prepillin peptidase PilD.
source: The PilQ secretin (orange) forms a channel in the outer membrane for secretion of the pilus-forming protein PilA4 (green), which is processed by the prepillin peptidase PilD (grey) (Friedrich et al., 2002; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by citations to Friedrich et al., 2002; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: The membrane protein PilW plays a role in DNA transport, PilQ assembly, and pilus extrusion.
source: The membrane protein PilW (light orange) plays a role in DNA transport, PilQ assembly, and pilus extrusion (Rumszauer et al., 2006; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by citations to Rumszauer et al., 2006; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: The dimeric complex PilC is located in the inner membrane and is essential for pilus formation.
source: The dimeric complex PilC (red) is located in the inner membrane and is essential for pilus formation (Friedrich et al., 2002; Karuppiah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by citations to Friedrich et al., 2002; Karuppiah et al., 2010.

claim: PilM, PilN, and PilO are suggested to form the inner membrane assembly platform and connect the periplasmic and cytoplasmic sides of the complex.
source: PilM (light brown), PilN (dark brown), and PilO (beige) are suggested to form the inner membrane assembly platform and connect the periplasmic and cytoplasmic sides of the complex (Rumszauer et al., 2006; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009; Karuppiah and Derrick, 2011; Karuppiah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by citations to Rumszauer et al., 2006; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009; Karuppiah and Derrick, 2011; Karuppiah et al., 2013.

claim: The cytoplasmic ATPases PilF and PilT1/PilT2 drive pilus extension and retraction, respectively.
source: The cytoplasmic ATPases PilF (bright yellow) and PilT1/PilT2 (pale yellow) drive pilus extension and retraction, respectively (indicated with red arrows) (Rose et al., 2011; Salzer et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by citations to Rose et al., 2011; Salzer et al., 2014b.

claim: Pili are several micron-long flexible filaments.
source: Pili are several micron-long flexible filaments (Craig and Li, 2008) that can generate forces of over 100 pN (Maier et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Craig and Li, 2008.

claim: T4P can generate forces of over 100 pN.
source: Pili are several micron-long flexible filaments (Craig and Li, 2008) that can generate forces of over 100 pN (Maier et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maier et al., 2004.

claim: T4P are grouped together in a class based on the production and secretion of the major pilin protein PilA4.
source: T4P are grouped together in a class based on the production and secretion of the major pilin protein PilA4 (Thermus nomenclature), thousands of copies of which form the helical pilus (Craig et al., 2004; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Craig et al., 2004; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: Thousands of copies of PilA4 form the helical pilus.
source: T4P are grouped together in a class based on the production and secretion of the major pilin protein PilA4 (Thermus nomenclature), thousands of copies of which form the helical pilus (Craig et al., 2004; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Craig et al., 2004; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: T4P is the only known bacterial pilus that can be retracted rapidly.
source: The T4P is the only known bacterial pilus that can be retracted rapidly (Maier et al., 2004) to enable motility and adherence (Merz et al., 2000), major contributors to bacterial virulence (Hahn, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maier et al., 2004.

claim: T4P retraction enables motility and adherence.
source: The T4P is the only known bacterial pilus that can be retracted rapidly (Maier et al., 2004) to enable motility and adherence (Merz et al., 2000), major contributors to bacterial virulence (Hahn, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Merz et al., 2000.

claim: Motility and adherence are major contributors to bacterial virulence.
source: The T4P is the only known bacterial pilus that can be retracted rapidly (Maier et al., 2004) to enable motility and adherence (Merz et al., 2000), major contributors to bacterial virulence (Hahn, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hahn, 1997.

claim: Assembly and disassembly of the pilus is driven by the AAA-ATPases PilF (extension) and PilT1/PilT2 (retraction).
source: Assembly and disassembly of the pilus is driven by the AAA-ATPases (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) PilF (extension) and PilT1/PilT2 (retraction) (Salzer et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Salzer et al., 2014b.

claim: Mature PilA4 assembles into pili extending from the inner membrane by action of PilF.
source: It has been suggested that mature PilA4 assembles into pili extending from the inner membrane by action of PilF (Collins et al., 2013; Salzer et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2013; Salzer et al., 2014b.

claim: The outer membrane channel of the T4P machinery is formed by the dodecameric approximately 1 MDa secretin complex PilQ.
source: The outer membrane channel of the T4P machinery is formed by the dodacemeric ∼1 MDa secretin complex PilQ (Burkhardt et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: PilM, PilN, and PilO are hypothesized to be a central part of the pilus assembly platform and may couple the cytoplasmic and periplasmic sides of the T4P machinery.
source: Other proteins, in particular PilM, PilN, and PilO, are hypothesized to be a central part of the pilus assembly platform and may couple the cytoplasmic and periplasmic sides of the T4P machinery (Karuppiah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Karuppiah et al., 2013.

claim: Some proteins of the T4P complex have been implicated to play a dual role in both pilus assembly and natural competence.
source: Some proteins of the complex have been implicated to play a dual role in both pilus assembly and natural competence (Friedrich et al., 2002; Averhoff and Friedrich, 2003; Friedrich et al., 2003; Rumszauer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedrich et al., 2002; Averhoff and Friedrich, 2003; Friedrich et al., 2003; Rumszauer et al., 2006.

claim: T4P themselves are not directly involved in DNA uptake.
source: Recent results indicate that T4P themselves are not directly involved in DNA uptake (Burkhardt et al., 2012; Salzer et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2012; Salzer et al., 2014a.

claim: T4P are essential for pathogenesis by mediating adhesion, biofilm formation, and twitching motility.
source: T4P are essential for pathogenesis by mediating adhesion, biofilm formation, and twitching motility (Burrows, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burrows, 2012.

claim: Both secretins and T4P play important roles in virulence of different pathogenic bacteria, which has fostered their use as new targets for drug development.
source: Thus, both secretins and T4P play important roles in virulence of different pathogenic bacteria, which has fostered their use as new targets for drug development (Baron, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baron, 2010.

claim: There is no information on the in situ structure of either the T4P machinery or DNA translocator prior to this study.
source: To date, there is no information on the in situ structure of either the T4P machinery or DNA translocator.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Electron cryo-tomography has the unique ability to determine protein structures in cells at molecular resolution.
source: Electron cryo-tomography (cryoET) has the unique ability to determine protein structures in cells at molecular resolution.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the capabilities of cryoET.

claim: T. thermophilus has an unusual cell architecture with deep surface clefts formed by invaginations of the outer membrane.
source: T. thermophilus has an unusual cell architecture with deep surface clefts, formed by invaginations of the outer membrane (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By cryoET, the clefts in T. thermophilus are seen to be constrictions that run around the cell body.
source: By cryoET, these clefts are seen to be constrictions that run around the cell body (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Numerous fibrous and straight pili extend from the cell distal to the most polar outer membrane ring.
source: Distal to the most polar outer membrane ring, numerous fibrous and straight pili extend from the cell (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The pili are clearly associated with large protein complexes crossing the approximately 70 nm periplasm.
source: The pili are clearly associated with large protein complexes crossing the ∼70 nm periplasm (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The distribution of pili and PilQ is in line with previous fluorescence and electron microscopy data demonstrating polar localization.
source: This distribution is in line with previous fluorescence and electron microscopy data, which demonstrate the polar localization of PilQ (Seitz and Blokesch, 2013) and pili (Salzer et al., 2014c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seitz and Blokesch, 2013 and Salzer et al., 2014c.

claim: The periplasm of T. thermophilus cells is extraordinarily wide.
source: The periplasm of T. thermophilus cells is extraordinarily wide (Quintela et al., 1995; Castan et al., 2002) and too dense to select subvolumes for subtomogram averaging reliably.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quintela et al., 1995; Castan et al., 2002.

claim: The periplasm of T. thermophilus is too dense to select subvolumes for subtomogram averaging reliably.
source: The periplasm of T. thermophilus cells is extraordinarily wide (Quintela et al., 1995; Castan et al., 2002) and too dense to select subvolumes for subtomogram averaging reliably.
evidence: This is based on the authors' observations during data analysis.

claim: Cells were treated with 100 mM EDTA and pipetted to render the outer membrane leaky.
source: Therefore, cells were treated with 100 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and pipetted in order to render the outer membrane leaky (Caston et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used, supported by a citation to Caston et al., 1988.

claim: EDTA treatment and pipetting depleted the periplasm of most small proteins.
source: This had the desired effect of depleting the periplasm of most small proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: Sample preparation by EDTA treatment and pipetting removed the pilus from the complex.
source: Sample preparation by this method also removed the pilus from the complex, the empty T4P machinery was nonetheless still clearly visible (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The structure of the entire T4P complex was determined by subtomogram averaging.
source: We determined by subtomogram averaging the structure of the entire complex and found features distinct from those of the T2SS and T3SS secretins (Marlovits et al., 2006; Hodgkinson et al., 2009; Reichow et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the data and comparison to cited structures.

claim: The T4P machinery has features distinct from those of the T2SS and T3SS secretins.
source: We determined by subtomogram averaging the structure of the entire complex and found features distinct from those of the T2SS and T3SS secretins (Marlovits et al., 2006; Hodgkinson et al., 2009; Reichow et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison to structures cited from Marlovits et al., 2006; Hodgkinson et al., 2009; Reichow et al., 2010.

claim: The resolution obtained by averaging approximately 4000 particle subvolumes was approximately 35 Å.
source: The resolution obtained by averaging ∼4000 particle subvolumes was ∼35 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), most likely limited by the inherent flexibility of the complex (Burkhardt et al., 2011) and the difficulty of correcting precisely the contrast transfer function (CTF) for thick specimens.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The resolution is most likely limited by the inherent flexibility of the complex and the difficulty of correcting precisely the contrast transfer function for thick specimens.
source: The resolution obtained by averaging ∼4000 particle subvolumes was ∼35 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), most likely limited by the inherent flexibility of the complex (Burkhardt et al., 2011) and the difficulty of correcting precisely the contrast transfer function (CTF) for thick specimens.
evidence: This is an inference based on known limitations of the technique and a citation to Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: Subtomogram average maps show the central protein channel is approximately 35 nm long and approximately 15 nm wide.
source: Subtomogram average maps show the central protein channel (∼35 nm long and ∼15 nm wide) made up of several ring-shaped domains inserted into the outer membrane (Figure 3C, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The central protein channel is made up of several ring-shaped domains inserted into the outer membrane.
source: Subtomogram average maps show the central protein channel (∼35 nm long and ∼15 nm wide) made up of several ring-shaped domains inserted into the outer membrane (Figure 3C, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A 2D projection of the channel part of the subtomogram average was compared with projections of purified, negatively stained PilQ.
source: We compared a 2D projection of the channel part of the subtomogram average with projections of purified, negatively stained PilQ only (Burkhardt et al., 2011) (Figure 3C, central and right panels).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C, with reference to Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: PilQ consists of a C-terminal trapezoid 'cone structure' with staggered rings in the N-terminal domain.
source: PilQ was seen to consist of a C-terminal trapezoid 'cone structure' with staggered rings in the N-terminal domain (Burkhardt et al., 2011), in excellent agreement with our in situ structure.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burkhardt et al., 2011 and comparison to the current data.

claim: The in situ structure of PilQ is in excellent agreement with the structure of purified, negatively stained PilQ.
source: PilQ was seen to consist of a C-terminal trapezoid 'cone structure' with staggered rings in the N-terminal domain (Burkhardt et al., 2011), in excellent agreement with our in situ structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison between the current data and Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: The cryoET structure shows additional protein densities extending from the putative N0 domain of PilQ through the peptidoglycan layer to the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Moreover, the new cryoET structure shows additional protein densities extending from the putative N0 domain of PilQ through the peptidoglycan layer (P1 and P2) to the cytoplasmic membrane (C1) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Candidate proteins for the additional densities include PilW and PilO/PilN heterodimers.
source: Candidate proteins include PilW, which is associated with the inner and outer membranes and is essential for the outer membrane localization of PilQ (Rumszauer et al., 2006), and PilO/PilN heterodimers that could connect PilQ to the ATPases by PilM in the cytoplasm (Karuppiah and Derrick, 2011; Karuppiah et al., 2013) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on inference from known protein functions cited from Rumszauer et al., 2006; Karuppiah and Derrick, 2011; Karuppiah et al., 2013.

claim: These proteins are most likely connected to one another by flexible domains that are not well contrasted in the subtomogram average.
source: These proteins are most likely connected to one another by flexible domains that are not well contrasted in the subtomogram average.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that connections are not visible in the structure.

claim: A longitudinal slice through the complex reveals that PilQ has two gates which are closed in the absence of a pilus.
source: A longitudinal slice through the complex reveals that PilQ has two gates, which are closed in the absence of a pilus (Figure 3C, left panel and Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Gate 1 is formed by the 'cone' in the outer membrane.
source: Gate 1 is formed by the 'cone' in the outer membrane and gate 2 by the N1 domain at the base of PilQ, enclosing an empty periplasmic vestibule (Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Gate 2 is formed by the N1 domain at the base of PilQ.
source: Gate 1 is formed by the 'cone' in the outer membrane and gate 2 by the N1 domain at the base of PilQ, enclosing an empty periplasmic vestibule (Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The two gates enclose an empty periplasmic vestibule.
source: Gate 1 is formed by the 'cone' in the outer membrane and gate 2 by the N1 domain at the base of PilQ, enclosing an empty periplasmic vestibule (Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The C-terminal 'cone' has been shown to form an SDS-stable sub-domain.
source: The C-terminal 'cone' has been shown to form a sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-stable sub-domain (Burkhardt et al., 2011), thus, it is plausible that gate 1 is responsible for maintaining the integrity of the cell membrane in the closed state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: It is plausible that gate 1 is responsible for maintaining the integrity of the cell membrane in the closed state.
source: The C-terminal 'cone' has been shown to form a sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-stable sub-domain (Burkhardt et al., 2011), thus, it is plausible that gate 1 is responsible for maintaining the integrity of the cell membrane in the closed state.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the SDS-stable nature of the cone structure.

claim: A second gate formed by the N-terminal domains has not been observed in other secretins.
source: A second gate formed by the N-terminal domains has not been observed in other secretins (Korotkov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Korotkov et al., 2011.

claim: The N-terminus of PilQ forms an unusual βββαββ fold, different from the conserved ring-building βαββα folds.
source: The N-terminus of PilQ forms an unusual βββαββ fold, different from the conserved ring-building βαββα folds (Burkhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burkhardt et al., 2012.

claim: The unusual βββαββ fold may form part of gate 2.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that this motif may form part of gate 2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural features observed.

claim: To determine the structure of the T4P machinery in the open state, the pipetting step during sample preparation was omitted.
source: To determine the structure of the T4P machinery in the open state, the pipetting step during sample preparation was omitted ('Materials and methods'), which reduced the shearing forces and kept the assembled pilus intact (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Omitting the pipetting step reduced the shearing forces and kept the assembled pilus intact.
source: To determine the structure of the T4P machinery in the open state, the pipetting step during sample preparation was omitted ('Materials and methods'), which reduced the shearing forces and kept the assembled pilus intact (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Close inspection of the pilus shows a periodic structure.
source: Close inspection of the pilus shows a periodic structure (Figure 4C), which was suitable for subtomogram averaging.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ice surrounding the pili was thin (approximately 100 nm), making it possible to apply CTF-correction.
source: Since the ice surrounding the pili was thin (∼100 nm), it was possible to apply CTF-correction.
evidence: This is an observation about the sample conditions that enabled a specific analysis method.

claim: The structure of the pilus was determined at approximately 32 Å resolution by averaging 740 subvolumes.
source: The structure of the pilus was determined at ∼32 Å resolution by averaging 740 subvolumes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Power spectra calculated from a single tomographic slice or from the subtomogram average revealed a repeat distance of approximately 4.9 nm.
source: Power spectra calculated from a single tomographic slice or from the subtomogram average revealed a repeat distance of ∼4.9 nm (Figure 4C, lower panels).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The T. thermophilus pilus forms a right-handed helix of approximately 3 nm diameter.
source: The T. thermophilus pilus forms a right-handed helix of ∼3 nm diameter (Figure 4D), which is different from the previously determined electron cryo-microscopy structure of the isolated Neisseria gonorrhoeae T4P (Craig et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The T. thermophilus pilus structure is different from the previously determined electron cryo-microscopy structure of the isolated Neisseria gonorrhoeae T4P.
source: The T. thermophilus pilus forms a right-handed helix of ∼3 nm diameter (Figure 4D), which is different from the previously determined electron cryo-microscopy structure of the isolated Neisseria gonorrhoeae T4P (Craig et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on comparison to the structure cited from Craig et al., 2006.

claim: Diameters of pili can vary considerably.
source: Diameters of pili can vary considerably and pilin proteins have limited sequence similarity (Craig and Li, 2008), which likely accounts for this difference.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Craig and Li, 2008.

claim: Pilin proteins have limited sequence similarity.
source: Diameters of pili can vary considerably and pilin proteins have limited sequence similarity (Craig and Li, 2008), which likely accounts for this difference.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Craig and Li, 2008.

claim: The variation in pilus diameter and limited sequence similarity likely accounts for the difference between T. thermophilus and N. gonorrhoeae pilus structures.
source: Diameters of pili can vary considerably and pilin proteins have limited sequence similarity (Craig and Li, 2008), which likely accounts for this difference.
evidence: This is an inference based on known structural variation and the citation to Craig and Li, 2008.

claim: The structure of the open T4P machinery with the pilus extended was determined from approximately 300 particles at approximately 45 Å resolution.
source: Due to the more challenging sample preparation method, the structure of the open T4P machinery with the pilus extended was determined from only ∼300 particles at ∼45 Å resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The resolution of approximately 45 Å is sufficient to reveal the central protein channel complex with the approximately 3 nm pilus protein density in the centre.
source: This resolution is sufficient to reveal the central protein channel complex with the ∼3 nm pilus protein density in the centre (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: An extensive conformational change shifts PilQ domains N0–N3 away from N4/N5 by approximately 30 Å towards the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: An extensive conformational change is evident that shifts PilQ domains N0–N3 away from N4/N5 by ∼30 Å towards the cytoplasmic membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4E and 5A,B.

claim: The conformational change opens the periplasmic vestibule to make way for the pilus.

These subtomogram averages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) show clearly that the same large conformational changes occur in the T4P machinery, irrespective of the degree of periplasmic protein depletion, and hence of the effect of EDTA.

claim: The T4P machinery tends to be tightly packed, with an inter-particle distance of 30–40 nm.

claim: The idle complexes may form a second class of transporter, which may be active in DNA uptake or protein secretion.

claim: T. thermophilus HB27 was grown in TM+ medium.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by a citation to Oshima and Imahori, 1971.

claim: Cells from a 24-hr pre-culture were transferred onto TM+ plates and incubated under humid conditions for 48 hr at 68°C.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Tomograms were typically collected from +60° to −60° at tilt steps of 2° and 5–7 μm underfocus.
source: Tomograms were typically collected from +60° to −60° at tilt steps of 2° and 5–7 μm underfocus, using either a Tecnai Polara or Titan Krios microscope (FEI, Hillsboro, USA), both equipped with field-emission guns operating at 300 kV and Quantum energy filters (Gatan, Pleasanton, USA) operated at a slit width of 20 eV.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Both microscopes were fitted with K2 Summit direct electron detector cameras.
source: Both instruments were fitted with K2 Summit direct electron detector cameras (Gatan, Pleasanton, USA).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment.

claim: The total dose per tomogram was approximately 140e−/Å2.
source: The total dose per tomogram was ∼140e−/Å2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters.

claim: Tomograms were aligned using gold fiducial markers and volumes reconstructed by weighted back-projection using the IMOD software.
source: Tomograms were aligned using gold fiducial markers and volumes reconstructed by weighted back-projection using the IMOD software (Boulder Laboratory, Boulder, USA) (Kremer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method, supported by a citation to Kremer et al., 1996.

claim: Contrast was enhanced by non-linear anisotropic diffusion (NAD) filtering in IMOD.
source: Contrast was enhanced by non-linear anisotropic diffusion (NAD) filtering in IMOD (Frangakis and Hegerl, 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method, supported by a citation to Frangakis and Hegerl, 2001.

claim: T. thermophilus PilQ is a dodecamer.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2011; Collins et al., 2003, 2004.

claim: 12-fold symmetry was applied to the core complex by 30° rotation of each subvolume prior to the alignment search.

evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: The final averages were obtained from 3984 particles for the closed complex and 312 particles for the open complex.
source: The final averages were obtained from 3984 particles for the closed complex and 312 particles for the open complex, using a mask drawn around PilQ.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: For the pilus, 740 subvolumes of approximately 2 nm length were selected from unbinned CTF-corrected tomograms.

evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: Resolution estimates were obtained using conventional 'even/odd' Fourier shell correlation (FSC), applying the 0.5 FSC criterion.
